primary_source.title: Aerosol generation by raindrop impact on soil

secondary_sources.title: Nature of Argillaceous Odour
secondary_sources.access_note: Publisher page verified (authors, CSIRO Melbourne affiliation, volume/pages, 7 March 1964). Full text is paywalled; the naming passage and the steam-distilled yellowish oil are verified against CSIRO's own institution article quoting the paper verbatim (https://www.csiro.au/en/news/All/Articles/2015/March/the-smell-of-rain-how-our-scientists-invented-a-new-word).

review_method: Joung & Buie 2015 read in full via the open-access publisher page (Nature Communications is online-only, article 6083, no print pagination; locators name the exact section/figure). Bear & Thomas 1964 verified at metadata level on the publisher page plus CSIRO's direct quotations of the paper; claims from it are limited to what those quotations state. The petrichor scent is named by the 2015 paper only as a possible implication; the aerosol-carries-the-scent link is the authors' hypothesis (MIT News, 14 Jan 2015) and is hedged in scene 8.

claims.paraphrase: In 1964, two Australian scientists (I. J. Bear and R. G. Thomas, CSIRO, Melbourne) named the smell petrichor, from an oil that accumulates in dry soil and rock.
claims.printed_page_locator: Nature 201, 993-995 (naming passage quoted verbatim by CSIRO; full text paywalled)
claims.support_summary: Publisher page confirms Bear & Thomas, CSIRO Division of Mineral Chemistry, Nature 201:993-995, 7 March 1964. CSIRO quotes the paper: 'propose the name petrichor ... ichor or tenuous essence derived from rock or stone', and describes steam-distilling warm dry-exposed rocks to a yellowish oil released by moisture.

claims.paraphrase: The team ran roughly 600 drop-impingement experiments on 28 porous media: 16 soils, 5 TLC plates and 7 porous titania films.
claims.printed_page_locator: Results: Characterization of aerosol generation; Methods: Preparation and characterization of porous media (Nat. Commun. 6:6083, online-only)
claims.support_summary: Paper states 'In total we conducted roughly 600 experiments' and 'We used 28 different porous medium samples' (16 soils incl. 8 collected around MIT campus/Charles River/Nahant Beach, 5 TLC plates, 7 titania films), with four liquids.

claims.paraphrase: In 2015, MIT researchers Young Soo Joung and Cullen R. Buie filmed droplet impacts with high-speed cameras.
claims.printed_page_locator: Title/author block and Results: Aerosol generation from droplets hitting soils (Nat. Commun. 6:6083, published 14 January 2015)
claims.support_summary: Both authors are MIT (affiliation 1; MIT News 14 Jan 2015 confirms). Paper: 'High-speed imaging provides visual proof of aerosol generation when liquid water droplets hit soil at velocities consistent with rainfall.'

claims.paraphrase: A raindrop flattens on porous ground, traps tiny air bubbles that grow with air from the pores, rise and burst at the drop's surface, ejecting jets that break into aerosol droplets.
claims.support_summary: Three-step process: bubble formation, growth, bursting. 'Tiny bubbles are trapped at the droplet/surface interface because the droplet expansion speed is faster than the water-absorption speed'; bubbles burst at the air-water interface, 'ejecting small jets that breakup into tiny droplets'.

claims.paraphrase: The aerosols carry material from the surface: dye placed in the pores was detected on glass slides above the impact site.
claims.printed_page_locator: Results: Delivery of materials in porous media with aerosols; Methods: Delivery of materials in porous media with aerosol (Nat. Commun. 6:6083)
claims.support_summary: Rhodamine B in the pores of TLC plates; fluorescent spots counted on transparent glass above, shifting downstream with airflow: 'particulate matter within the porous surface can be convectively dispersed as aerosols generated from drop impingement.'

claims.paraphrase: Aerosol generation was verified for light and moderate rain on clay-like soils; it was not observed on sand or in conditions consistent with heavy rainfall.
claims.printed_page_locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'From the characterization map we conclude' (Nat. Commun. 6:6083)
claims.support_summary: 'We verified aerosol generation experimentally for conditions consistent with light and moderate rain on soil with similar water-absorption properties as clay and sandy clay soil. Aerosol generation was not observed on sand or during conditions consistent with heavy rainfall.' Light rain Uo<4.0 m/s, heavy rain Uo>7.0 m/s.

claims.paraphrase: The 2015 paper names petrichor as a possible implication of the aerosol mechanism; the scent riding the aerosols is the authors' hypothesis, not a measured result.
claims.printed_page_locator: Introduction, paragraph 2 (Nat. Commun. 6:6083); MIT News 14 January 2015
claims.support_summary: Paper: implications range 'to the earthy smell known as petrichor present after a rain shower on a hot day'. Buie in MIT News: 'One hypothesis we have is that that smell comes from this mechanism we have discovered.' The paper measures aerosols, not odor.

editorial_suggestions.text: Compare the bubble burst to champagne fizz (MIT News uses the same comparison).
Close by telling the viewer to notice the smell at the next light rain after a dry spell.
Phrase the scent link as 'the likely ride for the smell', attributed to the scientists, keeping the hypothesis honest.
End on 'you know what you're breathing' so the replay lands on the hook's 'You know that smell after rain?'
